Dislike something very strongly — Detestar / aborrecer.
v|Stronger than dislike. Pattern: detest doing something.
Smile or speak with scorn — Burlarse / mofarse.
He sneered at my old car.
A scornful look or remark — Mueca de desprecio.
Look angry with lowered eyebrows — Fruncir el ceño.
Think about something carefully — Considerar / pensar.
v|Pattern: consider doing something, never consider to do.
Cry loudly with grief or pain — Gemir / lamentarse.
A long sad cry — Lamento / gemido.
We heard the wail of a siren.
Something that stands for something else — Símbolo.
The dove is a symbol of peace.
Adjective: symbolic. Careful: a symbol is a sign, cymbals are musical plates.
The power to give orders — Autoridad.
Only the manager has that authority.
An expert on a subject — Autoridad / experto.
She is an authority on Roman law.
An official body, often plural — Autoridades.
Without strong colour or feeling — Neutro/a.
The walls are a neutral grey.
Something of little importance — Nimiedad / insignificancia.
A little bit — Un poco / un pelín.
The soup is a trifle salty.
The architect showed us the plans.
The person who creates something — Artífice.
She was the architect of the agreement.
The ch sounds like k. Noun: architecture.
The state of being married — Matrimonio.
Formal. Everyday English says marriage. Adjective: matrimonial.
The bags a traveller carries — Equipaje.
We left our baggage at the hotel.
Old feelings or problems carried along — Carga emocional.
He brings a lot of emotional baggage.
Uncountable: a piece of baggage. British English often says luggage.
Spend or waste foolishly — Derrochar / malgastar.
v|Pattern: squander money, time or a chance.
In or to another country — En el extranjero.
She studied abroad for a year.
No preposition before it: go abroad, not go to abroad.
Person running away from the law — Fugitivo/a / prófugo/a.
The fugitive was caught at the border.
A terrible event causing great loss — Calamidad / desastre.
The flood was a calamity for the village.
A very poor person — Indigente / pobre de solemnidad.
The talks collapsed after a week.
Bring someone to court — Procesar / enjuiciar.
The company was prosecuted for fraud.
v|Noun: prosecution. Careful: prosecute is to take to court, persecute is to treat cruelly.
Being married to two people at once — Bigamia.
A person who does it is a bigamist.
Able to happen or be done — Posible.
It is possible to finish today.
Force someone to do something — Obligar / forzar.
v|Pattern: compel someone to do something. Adjective: compelling.
A risky project, often in business — Empresa arriesgada / aventura.
The restaurant was a new venture.
Dare to do or say something — Atreverse a.
Causing wonder or respect — Imponente / impresionante.
The canyon is an awesome sight.
Very good, in informal speech — Genial / increíble.
The informal sense is very common in American English.
Person who shows the way — Guía.
A guide took us round the castle.
Show someone the way — Guiar / orientar.
She guided us through the market.
A book of advice or information — Guía.
Buy a guide to the city.
Satisfy thirst — Saciar / apagar la sed.
Water quenches thirst better than juice.
Put out a fire — Apagar / extinguir.
They quenched the flames with sand.
He did not utter a single word.
Bring peace to a region — Pacificar.
Troops were sent to pacify the area.
He responded to my letter at once.
The patient responded well to the treatment.
v|Noun: response. Pattern: respond to something.
Signal to someone with your hand or head — Hacer señas / llamar con la mano.
The waiter beckoned us to a table.
Interrupt something and stop it working — Interrumpir / alterar.
The storm disrupted the train service.
The waste gas from an engine — Escape / gases de escape.
Black smoke came from the exhaust.
v|Adjective: exhausted. Noun: exhaustion. The h is silent.
Being very strict or very serious — Severidad / gravedad.
The severity of the punishment shocked us.
His voice was feeble after the illness.
Join together and become one — Unir(se).
The two parties united against the plan.
Stop; come to an end — Cesar / dejar de.
v|Formal. Patterns: cease doing and cease to do. Phrase: cease-fire.
Mean about spending money — Tacaño/a / avaro/a.
From miser, a person who hoards money.
The ch sounds like k. Noun: monarchy.
